## Proof

**Claim:** The statement is **false**. Not every invertible linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over a finite field of characteristic $p$ satisfies $T^{p(p-1)} = I$.

We exhibit an explicit counterexample.

**Setup.** Take $p = 2$ and let $\mathbb{F}_2$ be the field with two elements. Let $V = \mathbb{F}_2^2$, a 2-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Consider the linear operator $T : V \to V$ represented (with respect to the standard basis) by the matrix

$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\mathbb{F}_2).$$

**$T$ is invertible.** The determinant is $\det A = 0 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot 1 = -1 \equiv 1 \pmod{2}$, which is nonzero in $\mathbb{F}_2$. Hence $A \in \mathrm{GL}(2, \mathbb{F}_2)$, so $T$ is an invertible linear operator on $V$.

**Compute $A^2$.** Working in $\mathbb{F}_2$:

$$A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0\cdot 0 + 1\cdot 1 & 0\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 1 \\ 1\cdot 0 + 1\cdot 1 & 1\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$

Since $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \neq \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I$, we have $A^2 \neq I$.

**Compute $A^3$ to confirm the order.**

$$A^3 = A^2 \cdot A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1\cdot 0 + 1\cdot 1 & 1\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 1 \\ 1\cdot 0 + 0\cdot 1 & 1\cdot 1 + 0\cdot 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I.$$

Thus $A$ has order exactly $3$ in $\mathrm{GL}(2, \mathbb{F}_2)$.

**Apply the proposed identity.** For $p = 2$, the exponent in question is $p(p-1) = 2 \cdot 1 = 2$. The claimed identity would require

$$T^{p(p-1)} = T^{2} = I.$$

But we have shown $A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \neq I$. Therefore

$$T^{p(p-1)} = T^2 \neq I,$$

contradicting the claimed identity.

**Conclusion.** The invertible linear operator $T$ on the finite-dimensional vector space $V = \mathbb{F}_2^2$ over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_2$ of characteristic $p = 2$ does **not** satisfy $T^{p(p-1)} = I$. Hence it is **not true** that every invertible linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over a finite field of characteristic $p$ satisfies $T^{p(p-1)} = I$.
